patch_description:
Fundamentally different paradigm: replace the lag-inducing "wide forward SG + recency-tilt compensation" architecture with **zero-phase bidirectional adaptive Kalman smoothing**. The prior design fights its own group delay: it widens the smoothing window (adding lag), then tries to claw lag back with an exponentially tilted window (adding bias and losing smoothness). Instead, I run the same capped-NIS adaptive constant-velocity Kalman filter twice — once forward, once on the time-reversed signal — and average the two. This is the classic forward-backward (RTS-style) trick: the backward pass contributes *negative* group delay that exactly cancels the forward pass's lag, so we get full smoothing-window noise suppression at near-zero phase. This directly attacks lag_error (0.47) and correlation (0.75) simultaneously, which the tilted-window approach could never do.

Second difference: the length contract (len(y) = n − W + 1) is met with a **symmetric (zero-phase) weighted window aggregation** instead of a recency-tilted one, so the contraction step itself adds no lag. Third, spurious reversals are attacked with a robust **local taut-string-style diff shrinkage**: diffs that oppose the local median trend and are insignificant vs. local MAD are snapped to the local median slope, then re-integrated and convex-blended — targeting slope_changes/false_reversals (the two heaviest weighted weaknesses) without an extra smoothing stage that would hurt responsiveness. Finally a 3-tap median (blended, always axis=1) kills isolated single-sample spikes at zero phase cost, per the validated recommendation.
